intro: The International Space Station is a vessel in which modules and trusses are connected by a single network of life support, power, and thermal management. Rather than memorizing names, grasp in three dimensions where water, air, and heat flow.
lessons.0.title: The Station is a collection of main lines and rooms
lessons.0.summary: Russian segment propulsion and initial power, U.S. segment experiments and regenerative life support, the International Laboratory, and truss power and thermal systems. See the roles first.
lessons.0.body.0: Since 1998, the ISS has been built as partners sequentially joined modules. Official station descriptions position it as a continuous crewed research laboratory and an orbital hub for international cooperation. When candidates use physical models or 3D visualizations, the goal is not to provide a tourist guide, but to imagine which hatches to close and which main lines remain during an anomaly.
lessons.0.body.1: The rough skeleton is as follows. The Russian segment (Zarya, Zvezda, etc.) handled initial propulsion, habitation, and docking. U.S. segment nodes (Unity, Harmony, Tranquility) serve as junctions for passageways and systems. Destiny, Columbus, and Kibo are laboratories. Quest is the airlock for U.S. spacesuits. The truss holds solar arrays and radiators.
lessons.0.body.2: The mini-game involves pointing to modules in 3D to connect the water and oxygen regeneration loops. Correct connections are not a test of memory, but a way to internalize the official configuration of the ECLSS and power systems.
lessons.0.facts.0.label: Start
lessons.0.facts.1.label: Perspective
lessons.1.title: Zarya was the first room and remains a junction
lessons.1.summary: The first Functional Cargo Block to reach orbit provided initial power, propulsion, and storage, connecting the U.S. and Russian segments.
lessons.1.body.0: Zarya (Functional Cargo Block) is the first element of the ISS. Official assembly history records that after its launch in November 1998, Unity was attached shortly thereafter, joining the U.S. and Russian segments into a single vessel. Initially, it supported attitude and altitude with solar arrays and propulsion, serving as a port for subsequent modules.
lessons.1.body.1: While primary propulsion and habitation have shifted to the Zvezda side, Zarya remains as a passageway, storage, and structural link between segments. Dismissing it as 'old because it was the first module' during an anomaly risks overlooking the valves and cables at the connection points.
lessons.1.body.2: Identifying clues include the short block on the Russian segment side and the mating interface with Unity. In 3D, be aware that the display language and some procedural instructions change at this boundary.
lessons.1.facts.0.label: Role
lessons.1.facts.1.label: Mating
lessons.2.title: Unity and Zvezda extended the ship's spine
lessons.2.summary: The first U.S. node and the Russian service module formed the skeleton for passageways, habitation, and propulsion.
lessons.2.body.0: Unity (Node 1) was the first U.S.-built module. With multiple docking ports, it became the branching point for subsequent U.S. segments, the truss, and Quest. A node is not merely a passageway; it is a junction where air, power, data, and cooling water intersect.
lessons.2.body.1: Zvezda is the service module that docked in 2000. It placed the core of initial permanent habitation, life support, propulsion, and communications in the Russian segment. Official crewed operations began in earnest with the first long-duration expedition following the Zvezda docking.
lessons.2.body.2: The reason to view these two modules in sequence is that the station is neither a 'U.S. laboratory' nor a 'Russian residence,' but rather has both main trunks in series. Emergency evacuation routes and propulsion reboost commands cannot be understood without grasping this spine.
lessons.3.title: Destiny is the primary U.S. laboratory
lessons.3.summary: A cylinder with 24 rack interfaces accommodates both the station's systems and science.
lessons.3.body.0: Official Destiny descriptions identify it as the primary U.S. payload laboratory, supporting a wide range of experiments related to health, safety, and quality of life. It has a mass of approximately 32,000 pounds, a length of 28 feet, and a diameter of 14 feet. The interior contains 24 rack positions, officially divided into 13 for science and 11 for systems.
lessons.3.body.1: Launched on February 7, 2001, and docked on February 10, during Assembly Flight 5A aboard the Space Shuttle Atlantis, with the crew of Expedition 1. The Window Observational Research Facility (WORF) provides windows for Earth observation, and the Microgravity Science Glovebox enables the safe handling of samples.
lessons.3.body.2: The ECLSS overview notes that a second air revitalization system is located in Destiny. The laboratory is not merely a room for experiments. It houses life support redundancy, the initial attachment point for the robotic arm (STS-100), and an Earth observation window.
lessons.3.facts.0.label: Racks
lessons.3.facts.1.label: Docking
lessons.4.title: Harmony, Tranquility, and Quest determine crew flow
lessons.4.summary: Nodes are docking intersections, and Quest is the airlock for U.S. spacesuits.
lessons.4.body.0: Harmony (Node 2) docks to the forward end of Destiny and serves as an intersection connecting Columbus, Kibo, and visiting vehicle docking ports. Tranquility (Node 3) houses life support racks, exercise equipment, and serves as the base for the cupola. Mistaking one node for another could lead a crew member intending to go to a laboratory into an airlock instead.
lessons.4.body.1: The official Quest overview describes the pressurized module as divided into two compartments. The Equipment Lock features systems for suit maintenance and repressurization, while the Crew Lock serves as the actual exit to the outside. It measures 18 feet in length, 13.1 feet in diameter, and has a mass of 21,877 pounds. It is the primary route for extravehicular activities using U.S. spacesuits and can also support the Russian Orlan suit.
lessons.4.body.2: Launched on July 12, 2001, and docked on July 15, 2001, this airlock was part of assembly flight 7A (STS-104). The official objectives of STS-100 state that operation of Canadarm2 was a prerequisite for installing it. Although the arm and the hatch appear to be separate subjects, they are sequential in the assembly order.
lessons.4.facts.1.label: Docking
lessons.5.title: Columbus and Kibo are different experimental languages in the same microgravity
lessons.5.summary: The European and Japanese laboratories feature internal racks and external experiment platforms, branching off from Harmony.
lessons.5.body.0: Columbus (ESA) and Kibo (JAXA) are international laboratories that dock to the left and right of Harmony, respectively. The official station overview positions partner laboratories as sharing the scientific workload of the ISS across multiple nations. Kibo is distinguished by its internal laboratory, external experiment platform, and its own robotic arm (JEMRMS).
lessons.5.body.1: Experimental procedures must simultaneously satisfy the safety review of the national space agency and the allocation of power, cooling, and communications for the entire ISS. Treating a rack as 'your country's room' causes you to overlook the main lines for heat and power. In the event of an anomaly, the priority is determining which experiments to stop to return power to life support.
lessons.5.body.2: Identification involves the large cylinder extending from Harmony and Kibo's external pallet. In 3D, verify the angle where the line of sight from the Cupola overlaps with the work surface outside Kibo.
lessons.5.facts.0.label: Docking Origin
lessons.6.title: The Cupola is a window to Earth and a cockpit for the arm
lessons.6.summary: The seven windows are not just for tourism. The robotics workstation serves as the eyes for capturing resupply vehicles.
lessons.6.body.0: The Cupola is an observation module docked to Tranquility. It features six side windows and one Earth-facing window, and in official daily operations, a robotics workstation for operating the robotic arm is placed there. Earth observation and visual tracking of approaching resupply vehicles overlap at the same station.
lessons.6.body.1: The windows are structural components and are also subject to debris and solar exposure management. The timing for closing the shutters changes depending on sleep, extravehicular activities, and visiting vehicle approaches. One must switch between the act of viewing the beautiful Earth and the act of trusting the arm's cameras in the same location.
lessons.6.body.2: The PMM (Permanent Multipurpose Module, formerly the Logistics Module) remains in the U.S. segment as a storage room. While the Cupola's 'viewing' and the PMM's 'storing' are unglamorous, they are effective for the quality of life during long-duration stays and for ensuring clear pathways in emergencies.
lessons.6.facts.0.label: Windows
lessons.6.facts.1.label: Usage
lessons.7.title: The Truss is a power plant and a heat sink
lessons.7.summary: Solar arrays, radiators, and the ammonia loop enable experiments and life support inside the station.
lessons.7.body.0: The Integrated Truss Structure is a beam extending outside the module row. Solar arrays generate power, batteries support the night side, and large radiators dissipate heat. The working fluid of the external cooling system is ammonia, and leaks become toxic incidents addressed in later emergency modules.
lessons.7.body.1: Power is not just about 'having enough.' Voltage systems, channel separation, and allocation to experimental racks exist simultaneously. The orientation of solar arrays, the shadowing of radiators, and attitude control are mutually constrained.
lessons.7.body.2: The identifying clues are the long wings and white radiator panels. Translate the appearance seen in the scanning module into a system diagram here. If the wings stop, the next night side becomes dangerous; if heat rejection stops, life support will suffer from heat before the experiments do.
lessons.7.facts.0.label: Power
lessons.7.facts.1.label: Thermal
lessons.8.title: Water and oxygen cannot be supplied from Earth alone
lessons.8.summary: Regenerative life support recovers water from urine, sweat, and humidity, and produces oxygen by electrolyzing that water.
lessons.8.body.0: The official fact sheet, designed and tested by the Marshall Space Flight Center, describes ECLSS as consisting of three elements: water recovery, air revitalization, and oxygen generation. In the U.S. segment, four refrigerator-sized racks fit into Tranquility, with a second air revitalization system located in Destiny. Water recovery has been in continuous operation since 2008.
lessons.8.body.1: Official records state that the crew drinks approximately 0.5 gallons of water per day. ECLSS recovers 90 percent of sweat and urine (per the same fact sheet). Oxygen is obtained by electrolyzing water using power from the solar arrays. Hydrogen is separated, and the design philosophy includes routing a portion of it to subsequent reactions such as carbon dioxide reduction.
lessons.8.body.2: Official sources emphasize that resupply cannot keep up in deep space. The ISS regenerative systems also serve as prototypes for life support on the Moon and Mars. When connecting loops in the mini-game, do not resist the sequence urine → water → oxygen on emotional grounds; depict it as a system.
lessons.8.facts.0.label: Configuration
lessons.8.facts.1.label: Water Recovery
lessons.8.deepDive.title: Numbers can be revised
lessons.8.deepDive.body.0: Recovery rates may increase with equipment modifications. In operations, use the numbers from the latest procedures. In learning, first fix the three elements and configuration from the official fact sheet.
lessons.9.title: Canadarm2 is the hand for assembly and capture
lessons.9.summary: The 7-jointed arm attached to Destiny in 2001 enabled module mating and resupply vehicle capture.
lessons.9.body.0: Official records of STS-100 (Assembly 6A) state that Canadarm2 was attached from a pallet outside Destiny, 'walked' to the electrical grapple, and performed the first robot-to-robot handoff with the Shuttle's arm. The installation of Quest on the following flight, STS-104, was premised on the operation of this arm.
lessons.9.body.1: The arm can move along grapple fixtures. It is not a fixed crane, but a machine that walks on the surface of the ship. Detailed operation is deferred to the robotics module. Here, remember that power and communications depend on the systems of Destiny and the truss side.
lessons.9.body.2: The conclusion of the systems module is not a memorization test of module names. Water, air, power, heat, hatches, and arms. Be able to point out in 3D which rooms these six systems pass through.
lessons.9.facts.0.label: Attachment
lessons.9.facts.1.label: Initial Fixing
quiz.0.prompt: Which of the following is the first orbital element of the ISS?
quiz.0.explanation: Zarya was the first functional cargo block, and Unity was immediately attached to it, connecting the U.S. and Russian segments.
quiz.1.prompt: According to the official Destiny explanation, what is the total number of internal rack positions?
quiz.1.explanation: Destiny has 24 rack interfaces, officially broken down into 13 for science and 11 for systems.
quiz.2.prompt: What is the official dimension (length) of Destiny?
quiz.2.explanation: Official Quick Facts state a length of 28 feet, a diameter of 14 feet, and a mass of approximately 32,000 pounds.
quiz.3.prompt: Which of the following are the two compartments that officially constitute Quest?
quiz.3.explanation: Quest has an equipment lock for suit maintenance and a crew lock for exiting the ship, arranged in series.
quiz.4.prompt: What are the three elements listed in the official ECLSS fact sheet?
quiz.4.choices.0: Water recovery, Air revitalization, Oxygen generation
quiz.4.explanation: ECLSS is described by three main elements: Water Recovery, Air Revitalization, and Oxygen Generation.
quiz.5.prompt: According to the same fact sheet, what is the main configuration of U.S. segment ECLSS racks?
quiz.5.choices.1: 4 racks in Tranquility, second air revitalization in Destiny
quiz.5.explanation: Four refrigerator-sized racks are located in Tranquility, and a second Air Revitalization System is located in Destiny.
quiz.6.prompt: According to the official fact sheet, what is the water recovery rate from sweat and urine?
quiz.6.explanation: The fact sheet states that ECLSS recovers 90 percent of the sweat and urine produced by astronauts.
quiz.7.prompt: Which method does the official source describe for oxygen generation on the ISS?
quiz.7.choices.3: Electrolysis of water using power from solar arrays
quiz.7.explanation: Oxygen is produced by electrolysis, which splits water molecules into hydrogen and oxygen. The power comes from the station's solar arrays.
quiz.8.prompt: Which shuttle mission is officially credited with the launch and docking of Quest?
quiz.8.explanation: Quest was launched on July 12, 2001, and docked on July 15, 2001, during Assembly Mission 7A, STS-104.
quiz.9.prompt: Which official mission delivered Canadarm2 to the ISS?
quiz.9.explanation: STS-100 had the primary objective of installing, activating, and checking Canadarm2.
quiz.10.prompt: Which is the correct number of windows in the Cupola?
quiz.10.explanation: The Cupola has 6 side windows and 1 Earth-facing window, used for observation and robotic operations.
quiz.11.prompt: Which working fluid does this lesson emphasize for the external thermal control loop?
quiz.11.explanation: Heat from inside the station is transferred from the water loop to ammonia outside the station and then rejected via radiators. An ammonia leak would result in a toxic atmosphere event.
quiz.12.prompt: What is the official docking date for Destiny according to the Quick Facts?
quiz.12.explanation: Launched on February 7, docked on February 10, Assembly Mission 5A, STS-98. The crew staying was Expedition 1.
quiz.13.choices.1: Internal laboratory plus external experiment platform and JEMRMS
quiz.13.choices.2: Another name for the US airlock
quiz.13.explanation: JAXA's Kibo is an international laboratory module featuring internal experiments, an external platform, and its own robotic arm.
quiz.14.prompt: According to the official fact sheet, what is the approximate daily water consumption per crew member?
quiz.14.explanation: The fact sheet states that astronauts drink approximately 0.5 gallons of water per day, similar to people on Earth.
quiz.15.prompt: What robotic operation did the official STS-100 record describe as a 'first in history'?
quiz.15.choices.0: Remote driving of a lunar rover
quiz.15.choices.1: Atmospheric reentry of an unmanned aircraft
quiz.15.choices.3: Transfer between the station arm and the shuttle arm
quiz.15.explanation: Canadarm2 passing a cradle to the shuttle's arm was recorded as the first inter-robotic transfer.
glossary.0.term: Environmental Control and Life Support System
glossary.0.description: Regenerative life support centered on water recovery, air revitalization, and oxygen generation. The US segment primarily places racks in Tranquility.
glossary.1.description: The first module of the ISS. It provided initial power, propulsion, and storage, and connected Unity to the Russian segment.
glossary.2.description: The first US node. It serves as a junction branching to the US segment, the truss, Quest, and others via multiple ports.
glossary.3.description: The main US laboratory. It features 24 racks, an Earth observation window, a second air revitalization system, and initial arm attachment points.
glossary.4.description: A pressurized airlock consisting of an equipment lock and a crew lock. It is the primary path for US EMU extravehicular activities.
glossary.5.description: A node that houses ECLSS racks and exercise equipment, and serves as the base for the Cupola.
glossary.6.description: An observation module with 7 windows. It houses workstations for Earth observation and Canadarm2 operation.
glossary.7.description: A beam structure supporting solar arrays, batteries, radiators, and external cooling.
glossary.8.description: A 7-jointed station robotic arm used for assembly, maintenance, and capturing resupply vehicles.
